source.title: Scale-Invariance Drives Convergence in AI and Brain Representations
source.authors: Jun-Jie Yu; Wenxiao Ma; Jian-Yu Zhang; Hao-Tian Deng; Zihan Deng; Yi Guo; Quan-Ying Liu

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses representational convergence, but its experiments measure scale-invariance in vision-model embeddings and alignment with fMRI responses, not convergence between independently trained models or alignment between paired image and caption representations.
record.gate_note: The reported results are about AI-to-fMRI alignment and properties of embedding geometry. They do not directly measure model-to-model convergence, cross-modal image-caption convergence, or any other version in the claim. Adjacent findings are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The study cites the Platonic hypothesis as motivation but never measures similarity between independently trained models or between paired image and caption representations. It measures how ConvNeXt embeddings align with fMRI (ridge R2), plus within-model multi-scale geometry. Brain alignment of single models is a related but different construct from model-to-model convergence. Its title claim that scale-invariance drives convergence is a hypothesis, not a model-to-model test.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that compact, scale-invariant embedding structure predicts better visual-cortex fMRI alignment. They argue that large multimodal pretraining promotes this structure and label fine-tuning disrupts it. They frame scale-invariance as driving AI–brain convergence, but they do not measure convergence among AI models.
record.recipe_differences: The study does not reproduce the original model-to-model similarity methods; it analyzes multi-scale embedding geometry and AI-to-fMRI alignment instead.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported findings depend on the scale examined: dimensionality relates to alignment in opposite directions at smaller and larger scales. In the affine analysis, optimal transport changes whether the expected residual trend is observed. JS-divergence/alignment associations were reported as absent for Subjects 4 and 8 in the across-subject EBA analysis.

fits_no_version.finding: Flatter dimension slopes across k, lower affine residuals, and lower H1 JS divergence predict higher EBA fMRI alignment across 60 ConvNeXt models. Correlation reaches -0.816 at small k.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-scale geometric consistency of vision embeddings predicts their fit to visual-cortex fMRI.

fits_no_version.finding: Within ConvNeXt, larger pretraining data and CLIP-style language pretraining go with more scale-consistent geometry, and label fine-tuning reduces cross-scale similarity. Language-pretrained, non-fine-tuned models align best with EBA.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Pretraining data size and modality shape embedding geometry and brain alignment. The factors are not independently controlled.

fits_no_version.finding: fMRI manifolds show lower mid-to-large-scale dimension and stronger cross-scale self-similarity than AI embeddings.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Neural representations are more scale-invariant than ConvNeXt embeddings.

record.problems: The authors state that dataset size, modality, and fine-tuning are difficult to control simultaneously, limiting causal attribution. Most findings are qualitative in the text; many model-specific results appear in figures without numerical values. The study focuses on one brain region for its main analysis and uses one architecture family, ConvNeXt.
record.rows_left_out: No additional adjacent results were extracted from figures that are described only as supplementary replications across other ROIs or subjects; their text summaries repeat the qualitative findings already captured in R3, R7, and R9, without separate numerical values.

untested.parts: No model-to-model alignment as a function of scale or capability; only model-to-fMRI alignment.
No image–caption cross-modal alignment. The language-modality grouping (CLIP ConvNeXt) measures only the vision embeddings' fMRI fit and geometry.
No model-to-model mapping or stitching. Ridge maps go to voxels, not to other models.
No feature or circuit universality analysis.
No test of how a model-to-model convergence metric depends on its settings. The k-scale dependence shown concerns the link between intrinsic dimension and fMRI fit.
No measure of how complete model-to-model alignment is, or what causes it.

record.verdict_notes: All 60 models are ConvNeXt variants, so architecture is held fixed. Results are correlational. The study acknowledges that dataset size, modality and fine-tuning are confounded. The headline 'convergence' refers to AI–brain alignment, not to the model-to-model convergence the claim versions name.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test whether representations of independently trained AI models align more as model size or capability increases.
Does not measure alignment between vision and language representations of paired images and captions as both models improve.
Does not compare same-architecture networks trained from different initializations or test shared features or subspaces across seeds.
Does not test mapping, stitching, relative representations, or unpaired alignment between models.
Does not test whether interpretable features or circuits recur across models.
The study varies scales and methods for measuring embedding geometry, but does not test whether measured convergence between models depends on metric settings or inputs.
Does not test whether model-to-model alignment is incomplete or explained by shared training data or objectives.

rows.subject: all 60 pretrained vision models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Aligned model embeddings with fMRI responses using ridge regression and measured R2.
rows.note: This is aggregate AI-to-fMRI alignment, not similarity between models.
rows.check: Subject should say all 60 are ConvNeXt variants (Appendix B, Table 1), not generic vision models. The same correction applies to R3–R7 and R9.

rows.subject: ConvNeXt models grouped by pretraining modality and fine-tuning status (aggregate)
rows.stage_stated: pretrained; groups differ in fine-tuning status
rows.operation_detail: Compared fMRI alignment scores across model groups.

conditions.value: pretrained with language modality and without fine-tuning

rows.value: the language-pretrained, non-fine-tuned group significantly outperformed the other groups
rows.uncertainty: significance stated; numerical uncertainty not stated
rows.note: The outcome is alignment with fMRI, not cross-modal alignment between vision and language representations.

rows.subject: all 60 pretrained vision models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related the slope of estimated embedding dimension across neighborhood scales to fMRI alignment.
rows.measure: association between dimensional-slope flatness and fMRI alignment
rows.value: models with flatter dimensional slopes had stronger alignment
rows.note: The study reports a relationship between embedding geometry and brain alignment.

rows.subject: all 60 pretrained vision models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related mean estimated dimension across scales to fMRI alignment.
rows.measure: correlation of mean dimension with fMRI alignment
rows.uncertainty: significance stated; numerical uncertainty not stated
rows.note: The authors state that average dimensionality alone did not predict alignment.

rows.subject: all 60 pretrained vision models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related scale-specific estimated dimensions to fMRI alignment.
rows.measure: correlation between dimension and fMRI alignment
rows.note: Lower dimensions at smaller scales were associated with higher alignment.

rows.subject: all 60 pretrained vision models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related scale-specific estimated dimensions to fMRI alignment.
rows.measure: direction of association between dimension and fMRI alignment
rows.value: the relationship reversed: higher dimensions were associated with stronger alignment
rows.note: No coefficient for this scale range is stated.

rows.subject: all 60 pretrained vision models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measured affine residuals between embedding structures sampled at different scales and related them to fMRI alignment.

conditions.value: smallest-scale structure compared with larger scales

rows.measure: mean affine residual and residual slope versus fMRI alignment
rows.value: lower average residuals and flatter residual slopes were associated with higher alignment
rows.note: The relationship concerns model-to-fMRI alignment and cross-scale structure within embeddings.

rows.subject: best-aligned model and worst-aligned model (names not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared H1 feature birth-death scale distributions in model embeddings with those in EBA fMRI data.
rows.measure: H1 scale-distribution compactness and JS divergence relative to fMRI
rows.value: the best-aligned model had a more compact distribution resembling EBA; the worst-aligned model had a more diffuse distribution
rows.note: Model identities and numerical JS divergence values are not stated in the text.
rows.check: Best and worst models are unnamed in the text. Table 1 indexes models by EBA alignment, which implies M60 and M1, but the text does not confirm this.

rows.subject: all 60 pretrained vision models (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Related JS divergence between model and EBA H1 birth-death distributions to fMRI alignment.
rows.measure: correlation between JS divergence and fMRI alignment
rows.note: Lower divergence was associated with stronger alignment.

rows.subject: ConvNeXt models grouped by pretraining dataset size (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared scale-geometry measures across groups trained on datasets of different sizes.
rows.measure: average dimension, dimensional slope, and structural self-similarity across scales
rows.value: larger-dataset models had higher average dimensions, flatter dimensional slopes, and greater structural self-similarity
rows.note: The study notes that dataset size, modality, and fine-tuning were not fully controlled.

rows.subject: ConvNeXt models grouped by language-modality use (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared scale-geometry measures across models with and without language modality during pretraining.

conditions.value: pretraining with versus without language modality

rows.measure: dimensional slope and structural self-similarity across scales
rows.value: vision-language models had flatter dimensional slopes and stronger cross-scale consistency
rows.note: This compares within-model geometric properties and does not measure image-caption representation alignment.

rows.subject: ConvNeXt models grouped by fine-tuning status (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared scale-geometry measures across fine-tuned and non-fine-tuned model groups.
rows.measure: dimensional stability and structural self-similarity across scales
rows.value: fine-tuning did not explicitly alter dimensional stability but reduced cross-scale structural similarity
rows.note: The authors describe this as a partial disruption of multi-scale coherence.

rows.subject: embedding scale comparisons with and without optimal transport (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Compared affine residuals in multi-scale structural analysis with versus without optimal transport matching.
rows.baseline: with optimal transport, residuals decreased systematically as scales approached the smallest scale
rows.value: residuals remained consistently high across scales
rows.note: This is a comparison of measurement procedures, not a test of model-to-model convergence.
rows.check: This compares the study's own measurement procedure (with vs without optimal transport) and is not a result about the models. It arguably should not be a row, or should be marked as a method check.

rows.subject: fMRI data from visual cortical regions, Subject 1
rows.size_stated: 10,000 images per participant; voxel count varies by region
rows.operation_detail: Measured dimensionality and structural self-similarity across scales in voxel-response representations.
rows.measure: dimensionality and affine residuals across scales
rows.value: fMRI dimensionality rose rapidly at smaller scales, stabilized and remained lower at mid-to-large scales; fMRI had stronger structural self-similarity and lower affine residuals than AI embeddings
rows.note: This describes fMRI geometry relative to AI embeddings, not convergence among AI models.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
